#### What this PR does / why we need it:
In #118686, we make sure that wait.PollUntilContextTimeout function, if immediate is true, the condition will be invoked before waiting and guarantees that the condition is invoked at least once, regardless of whether the context has been cancelled. However, the changes in that pr will make new PollUntilContextCancel function immediately executes given condition twice, which is not mentioned anywhere. Which is not semantically same with wait.PollImmediateUntil.

Just for confirm that, it does mean the `wait.PollUntilContextCancel immediately`  have a wrong behavior? Thanks.

> Cleanup deprecated methods in wait package karmada-io/karmada#3835

According to #119533, `wait.PollUntilContextCancel immediately` will execute the condition twice at start, which is not semantically same with wait.PollImmediateUntil. 

And according to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119762#discussion_r1287386625 , we're having some issues with preserves sliding properly for the first iteration. Currently I'm waiting for @smarterclayton to tell me whether my [proposal](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119762#discussion_r1287423090) can fix this.

So the correctness of this function is ok, but we may have some timing issues.
Thanks for your clarify.

> we're having some issues with preserves sliding properly for the first iteration.

I think that this sliding problem is a bug we have in this and the previous implementation

I've updated the code and added a test case for sliding.
The logic of this case goes like this:

1. create a `loopConditionUntilContext`with a timer(one second each iteration), and a condition function(cost one second each time ), also with a context that will be canceld in 5 seconds.
2.  now if sliding is false,  then period includes the runtime for condition. So we'll never wait between two calls of the condition. Thus, we expected condition function to be called for 4 times.
3.  if sliding is true,  then period doesn't include the runtime for condition. So basically we will need two seconds for each iteration(one second to run contdition, and one second to wait the timer). And condition function should be called for 3 times.(It will finish the first two times, and get canceld when sleeping in third iteration).

I don't know if this case can ensures sliding isn't broken , I'd like to hear your opinions :)

issue_context.title: k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.PollUntilContextCancel immediately executes condition twice
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

While trying to update https://github.com/flatcar/flatcar-linux-update-operator/blob/7a1b0ff2769af91e8ff2bae82fc93f2f5baf0b0c/pkg/agent/agent.go#L328 to use latest version of `wait` package and to migrate away from deprecated `PollImmediateUntil`, function, our tests fail as it seems new `PollUntilContextCancel` function immediately executes given condition twice, which is not mentioned anywhere.

Result of executed test specified below:
```console
$ go test . -v
=== RUN   Test_test
=== PAUSE Test_test
=== CONT  Test_test
=== RUN   Test_test/PollUntilContextCancel
    prog_test.go:25: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:00 +0000 UTC m=+0.000000001
    prog_test.go:25: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:00 +0000 UTC m=+0.000000001
    prog_test.go:25: Unexpected early timestamp
=== RUN   Test_test/PollImmediateUntil
    prog_test.go:31: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:00 +0000 UTC m=+0.000000001
    prog_test.go:31: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:02 +0000 UTC m=+2.000000001
--- FAIL: Test_test (3.00s)
    --- FAIL: Test_test/PollUntilContextCancel (0.00s)
    --- PASS: Test_test/PollImmediateUntil (3.00s)
FAIL
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Since `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.PollImmediateUntil` has been deprecated and it recommends using `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.PollUntilContextCancel`, I expected it to have the equivalent semantics to allow easy migration from deprecated functions, as no changelog or documentation mentions new semantics.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Playground: https://go.dev/play/p/qQBnWM4nufF

Local:
1. `go mod init foo && go get k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait`
2. Create `main_test.go` file with the following content:
```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait"
)

const (
	testTimeout           = 3 * time.Second
	callsExpectedInterval = 2 * time.Second
)

func Test_test(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), testTimeout)
	t.Cleanup(cancel)

	t.Run("PollUntilContextCancel", func(t *testing.T) {
		f := testIntervals(t)

		wait.PollUntilContextCancel(ctx, callsExpectedInterval, true, func(context.Context) (bool, error) { f(); return false, nil })
	})

	t.Run("PollImmediateUntil", func(t *testing.T) {
		f := testIntervals(t)

		wait.PollImmediateUntil(callsExpectedInterval, func() (bool, error) { f(); return false, nil }, ctx.Done())
	})
}

func testIntervals(t *testing.T) func() {
	t.Helper()

	timestamps := make(chan time.Time, 1)

	timestamps <- time.Now().Add(-1 * 2 * callsExpectedInterval)

	return func() {
		t.Helper()

		t.Logf("Executed at %s", time.Now())

		if timestamp := <-timestamps; timestamp.After(time.Now().Add(-1 * callsExpectedInterval / 2)) {
			t.Fatalf("Unexpected early timestamp")
		}

		timestamps <- time.Now()
	}
}
```
3. Run as `go test . -v`.

review_comments: These variables (`immediate`,`sliding`)in for loop are never used, I wonder why we even have them?
use separete commits for these things please, so it it easier to review, so you don't add a new test, remove some dead code and modify the existing test in the same commit
How did you choose this amount to sleep?
Are you trying to cause it to race?

> Are you trying to cause it to race?

I explained my thoughts in [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119762#issuecomment-1671778866). 

Basically, I created a callback function which requires a long duration to execute. So in a same duration, poll with sliding true/false will execute this function different times.  

If sliding is false, we'll keep execute this function and never waits, because timech is drained during the sleep in condition function. Otherwise, we'll execute less times because we'll have to wait a longer time before next execution.

> How did you choose this amount to sleep?

Well, at first it was a big amount, and aojea suggests to reduce the time cost. So I tried to reduce it, but if this amount is too small, this test will fail in the CI(however it passed on my mac). I doubt it should be some accuracy problem. So I tried a few amounts, and this amount is ok on both sides(CI and my mac), and 1 second seems not too expensive.
it took me a while to understand it too, I had to draw it actually, it plays with the periods and the attempts to make it predictable
